candidates.title: Home-mixed skincare dispenser bypasses packaged SKUs
candidates.shift: A graduate-designed refillable dispenser lets consumers blend preservative-free skincare formulas at home from base ingredients, eliminating single-use packaged product SKUs.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: if this scales, beauty retail shelf space shifts from finished-good SKUs to ingredient cartridges — fewer facings, different inventory/insurance model, less packaging waste to manage in-store.
candidates.evidence: Meld system, a graduation project from Central Saint Martins, lets users combine ingredients to bypass toxic additives and packaging.
candidates.initial_analysis: This is an early example of retail shifting from packaged-product distribution to ingredient/format distribution at point of use, driven by sustainability and personalization pressure. If common, store layouts, SKU counts, and supply chains for beauty categories would need fundamental redesign.
candidates.author: Alyn Griffiths

candidates.title: Visitor center as remote retail/experience anchor
candidates.shift: A permanent exhibition/café/shop design for a geothermal visitor center in rural North Iceland treats retail and F&B as integrated infrastructure for extreme, low-density tourism sites.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: peripheral-geography instance of retail space being embedded into climate/geologic-hazard tourism infrastructure — may prefigure how retailers design small-footprint destination stores in remote or climate-exposed regions.
candidates.evidence: SP(R)INT STUDIO and Nissen Richards Studio completed exhibition, welcome area, café and shop design for Gígur Visitor Centre in North Iceland.
candidates.initial_analysis: A single project instance where retail/café/shop is fused into geologic-hazard tourism infrastructure rather than standalone commerce. Reflects a broader move of small-footprint, experience-anchored retail into remote or peripheral geographies as destination draws.
candidates.author: Cristina Popescu

candidates.title: Cafe as connective tissue between heritage site and new civic building
candidates.shift: A new café is designed explicitly as the physical hub linking a historic shrine to a newly built performing arts theater, positioning food/beverage space as civic connective infrastructure rather than a standalone retail unit.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: single instance of F&B space being deliberately programmed as the connective/community layer between old and new civic buildings — a reframing of café-as-retail into café-as-urban-infrastructure.
candidates.evidence: Cafe N+ by Horibe Associates designed as a hub connecting a historic shrine with a newly built performing arts theater in Takatsuki City, Japan.
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of café/retail space explicitly programmed as civic connective tissue rather than commercial destination in its own right — a reframing that could inform how retailers co-locate with cultural/civic infrastructure to anchor foot traffic.
candidates.author: Pratik Mour

candidates.title: Vertical circulation as retail's structuring device on narrow urban lots
candidates.shift: A single-level retail store is redistributed across three floors on a constrained urban lot, with vertical circulation treated as the primary organizing/design element rather than an afterthought.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: as urban land gets scarcer/pricier, retailers may increasingly need to 'go vertical' on narrow footprints — changing store operations, staffing patterns, and customer flow assumptions built around single-floor formats.
candidates.evidence: Panō Garcia Store in Ipanema (AIA Estúdio) redistributes a former single-level store program across three floors, with vertical circulation as the structuring element.
candidates.initial_analysis: A structural response to urban land scarcity: retail format shifting from single-floor to vertically stacked, with circulation as core design logic. If this becomes common in dense peripheral urban markets, staffing, layout, and customer-flow standards for stores would need rethinking.
candidates.author: Susanna Moreira

candidates.title: Raw-shell adaptive reuse as a build-out standard
candidates.shift: A restaurant fit-out deliberately leaves the existing concrete/steel building shell exposed rather than fully finishing it, minimizing renovation scope and material use.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: 'raw shell' minimal fit-out could become a construction-cost and embodied-carbon strategy for retail/F&B tenants in adaptive-reuse buildings — fewer trades, faster build-out, lower material spend, but also less brand-controllable interior.
candidates.evidence: Minnibar restaurant in Montreal by Ivy Studio 'embraces its raw shell' within a downtown high-rise's ground floor, using existing 20-foot ceilings rather than fully re-cladding.
candidates.initial_analysis: A single instance of a broader shift from full-finish tenant build-outs to raw/exposed-shell interiors, driven by embodied-carbon and cost pressure. If normalized, construction trades, materials specs, and lease build-out allowances for retail/F&B tenants would need to change.
candidates.author: Dan Howarth

candidates.title: Acoustic material engineering drives building envelope design
candidates.shift: A concert hall's copper cladding and dome form are engineered primarily as an acoustic instrument, not a facade choice — materials and structure driven by performance physics rather than aesthetics or cost alone.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative, off-map-adjacent: illustrates materials-as-function logic (envelope tuned to a physical performance metric) that could migrate to retail/logistics buildings tuned for noise, thermal, or acoustic performance rather than style.
candidates.evidence: PCA-Stream's La Source Vive, a 490-seat copper-clad domed concert hall in Évian, France, designed 'as a musical instrument.'
candidates.initial_analysis: An edge case of building envelopes engineered for a specific physical-performance metric (acoustics) rather than conventional aesthetic/cost logic — construction branch relevance if similar performance-tuned envelope thinking spreads to commercial/retail structures (thermal, noise, energy).
candidates.author: Rheanna Hopkins

candidates.title: Federal defunding of bike-lane infrastructure reframed as safety rollback
candidates.shift: The US federal government is cutting previously allocated cycling-infrastructure funding ($1.73bn), reframed by the administration as removing 'DEI bike lanes,' while advocates warn of reduced street safety.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: mobility-infrastructure funding is becoming politically contested/reversible rather than a stable planning input — retailers and developers relying on multimodal access (bike/ped traffic to storefronts) may need to hedge on infrastructure permanence.
candidates.evidence: Reported $1.73bn in previously allocated cycling-improvement funding for city streets being cut by the Trump administration; safety advocates dispute the framing and impact.
candidates.initial_analysis: Already-covered policy story (labeled Trend for Kristen's judgment) showing mobility infrastructure funding is now subject to rapid political reversal, not stable long-term planning input. Storefronts and developments banking on multimodal access/foot traffic may face policy volatility risk.
